newsitem.title: USA: Stocks end mixed, bonds rally after inflation data.
newsitem.headline: Stocks end mixed, bonds rally after inflation data.

text.p: Stocks ended mixed on profit-taking but bond prices jumped Friday -- sending interest rates lower -- after the government reported a surge in economic growth but little inflation at the end of last year.
The dollar fell against the Japanese yen but rose against the German mark. Oil prices tumbled and gold ended lower.
In the stock market, investors took profits in high-flying blue chips and shifted funds into small companies, boosting the lagging Nasdaq market.
The Dow Jones industrial average fell 10.77 points to 6,813.09 after racking up two straight days of gains. For the week, the index was up 116.61 points.
The Nasdaq composite index rose 8.83 points to 1,379.85, ending up 16.01 points for the week.
In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,380 to 1,098 on heavy volume of 574 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

"With a couple of good days behind us, it looks some players are taking profits ahead of the weekend," said Alan Ackerman, market strategist at Fahnestock & Co. "But it's modest and the market is giving back very little ground."
A strong rally in bonds on new evidence of tame inflation boosted blue-chip stocks earlier in the session but they fell victim to late profit-taking.

The good news came after the government said the economy grew at a strong 4.7 percent rate in the fourth quarter, more than double the third quarter rate of 2.1 percent, but that inflation gauges remained well in check.

In the inflation-sensitive bond market, the 30-year Treasury rose more than a full point, lowering its yield to 6.79 percent from 6.87 percent on Thursday. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
"Investors have been watching the yield on the long bond very carefully because many see 7 percent as a level where stocks may give back ground," said Ackerman.
"We did see a little profit-taking at the end, but with yields a bit lower there's a sense it's best to stay the course," he said.
Looking past the Dow's marginal decline, the signs from the stock market were mostly positive. According to market tradition, January's rise of 360 points on the Dow bodes well for 1997.
"As goes January, so goes the year," said Kenneth Ducey, director of trading at BT Brokerage, reciting a Wall Street adage.

The so-called "January Barometer" -- which by the purest method actually tracks the Standard & Poor's 500-stock index -- calls for the market to finish the year higher when it rises in January and lower when it falls in the month.

According to the research group the Hirsch Organisation, the barometer has forecast the market's direction in 41 of the last 46 years. The S&P 500 rose 1.99 to 786.16 Friday, capping a gain of 45.42 points or 6 percent for the month.
In currency markets, the dollar stood at 121.43 yen late in New York, down from 121.83 yen late on Thursday. Against the mark, the dollar edged higher to 1.6387 from 1.6363 at Thursday's close.
Oil prices fell as traders bet forecasts for milder weather in the Northeast would curtail demand for heating oil.

Heating oil for February delivery lost 1.69 cents to 68.65 cents a gallon and February gasoline fell 1.35 cents to 68.47 cents a gallon at the New York Mercantile Exchange. March crude oil fell 72 cents to $24.15 a barrel.

Overseas, Britain's FTSE index rose 47.4 points to a record 4,275.8 for a gain of 57 points for the week. Japan's Nikkei average of 225 shares jumped 465.97 points to 18,330.01, a rise of 640.65 on the week.
